topic: Compliance ops retainer vs. in-house CCO — when to use each
body:
The compliance question most $1M–$5M ARR fintechs face isn't "what do we need?" — it's "what's the minimum viable coverage that doesn't bankrupt us?"

The answer changes depending where you are:

**In-house CCO** — $150K–$250K/yr, full-time, available daily. Right choice when compliance activity exceeds ~40 hours/month consistently, or post-Series B. Wrong choice before you know what your actual compliance load looks like.

**Hourly outside counsel** — $200–$350/hr, event-driven. Right for discrete legal events: regulatory filings, enforcement responses, formal opinions. Structurally wrong for continuous monitoring and deadline tracking — the clock runs even when nothing's happening.

**Managed compliance ops retainer** — flat $2,500/mo. Covers: weekly regulatory brief, standing contract review on every vendor/DPA/SaaS agreement, filing deadline tracking (BOI, GDPR, VARA, MiCA), 24h async attorney Q&A, quarterly compliance health report.

What it doesn't cover: regulatory applications, litigation defense, formal opinions. Those stay with outside counsel.

Rough cost comparison for a fintech in 2–3 jurisdictions:
— In-house CCO: $180K–$250K/yr
— Hourly counsel (200–500 hrs): $40K–$120K/yr
— Retainer: $35K/yr ($5K setup + $2,500/mo)

The retainer isn't cheap. But it provides proactive coverage — monitoring, standing review, deadline alerts — that hourly counsel structurally can't deliver.

Transition point: most fintechs move to in-house CCO around $8M–$15M ARR when compliance volume justifies it. Below that, specialist retainer coverage usually beats a junior CCO without deep jurisdiction knowledge.
